name: Hair-removal epilator
lead: An epilator is an electric (or spring-powered) device that grips many hairs at once and pulls them out by the root as it passes over the skin. It works much like waxing but does not remove skin cells, and is used for legs, underarms, arms and, with small attachments, the face [1][2].

The first epilator was the original Epilady, made by Mepro at kibbutz HaGoshrim in Israel in 1986 [1]. Because hairs are removed below the surface, regrowth is generally described as taking longer than after shaving, though epilation does not permanently remove hair [1][2].
infobox: Mains or rechargeable; some wet/dry models [1]
Rated moderate to high, with the first session often the worst [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes a spring type, in which a motor-turned coil spring bent into a curve catches hairs; a rotating disc type, using metal discs; and a tweezer type, with plates that open and close as the head rotates to grip, pull and release hairs. Wet-use models can be used with water, and creams or gels are said to reduce pain and irritation. Heads may include smaller attachments for hard-to-reach areas or exfoliating heads [1].
Manual facial versions use a spring with two handles and no motor [1].

Per Wikipedia, the original Epilady used a coil spring and sold spare springs because they could fail. Remington's later model used metal discs instead, which led to European patent litigation including the 1990 UK case Improver Corp v Remington Consumer Products [1]. Grokipedia attributes the invention to Israeli engineers at Mepro and reports later rotating-disc designs from the mid-1990s [2].

Wikipedia says the first epilation typically yields less regrowth afterwards because of hair growth phases, and that some hairs snap off rather than being pulled out, leaving short stumps that are sparser than shaved hair. Regular use reduces the number of broken hairs [1]. Grokipedia reports results lasting up to about four weeks [2].

The first session is often the most painful. Wikipedia lists reducing device speed, relaxing the skin in a hot shower or bath, and applying numbing cream among ways people reduce discomfort, and lists initial pain, a learning curve and broken hairs as drawbacks [1]. Grokipedia reports that initial redness or ingrown hairs may occur, particularly in sensitive skin [2]. A review of laser and light therapies notes a rare side effect of paradoxical hypertrichosis after light-based epilation, which concerns a different method [3].

Epilators appear in appearance discussions mainly as a home option for body hair and small facial areas, positioned between shaving and clinic procedures such as laser or electrolysis. The sources reviewed contain no forum material, so community claims are not documented here.

Features described in the sources include tweezer or disc heads, adjustable speed, wet/dry operation, and attachments for the face or exfoliation [1][2]. Pain tolerance and skin sensitivity are listed as factors in how well the device is tolerated [1].

No studies found on consumer mechanical epilators. Published literature using the word epilator largely concerns needle electrolysis or laser and light devices, such as a histologic comparison of thermolysis methods [4].

card.summary: Handheld device that yanks hairs out by the root; slower regrowth than shaving, but painful and not permanent.
card.note: Pain is moderate to high, worst on the first session; ingrown hairs are possible.

quick.overview:
An epilator pulls many hairs out at the root as it moves over the skin, like a portable wax. Hair typically takes longer to return than after shaving, and regrowth is often finer and sparser.

The effect is temporary. No studies of consumer epilators were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: A motor drives spring coils, rotating discs or small tweezers that grip and extract hairs. Some hairs snap rather than pull out, leaving stumps.
quick.risks: Pain is the main drawback, usually worst on the first use. Redness and ingrown hairs can occur, especially on sensitive skin. Wet-use models and numbing creams are mentioned as ways people reduce discomfort.
